theory.overview: Single-qubit gates are unitary operations that rotate the qubit state on the Bloch sphere. They form the building blocks of quantum circuits. Every single-qubit gate can be represented as a 2×2 unitary matrix $U$ where $U^\dagger U = I$ (the identity). Geometrically, these gates rotate the Bloch vector around some axis. The most fundamental gates are the Pauli gates (X, Y, Z) which rotate by 180° around their respective axes, and the Hadamard gate which creates superposition by rotating around an axis at 45° between X and Z.

sections.title: The Pauli Gates
sections.content: The Pauli matrices are the quantum analogs of classical bit-flip and phase-flip operations. X (NOT gate) flips $|0angle \leftrightarrow |1angle$. Z flips the phase of $|1angle$ (leaving $|0angle$ unchanged). Y does both: it flips the bit AND adds a phase. Mathematically: $X = |0angle\langle 1| + |1angle\langle 0|$, $Z = |0angle\langle 0| - |1angle\langle 1|$, $Y = i|1angle\langle 0| - i|0angle\langle 1|$. On the Bloch sphere: X is a 180° rotation around X-axis, Y around Y-axis, Z around Z-axis. Importantly, $X^2 = Y^2 = Z^2 = I$—applying any Pauli gate twice returns to the original state.

sections.title: The Hadamard Gate
sections.content: The Hadamard gate ($H$) is arguably the most important single-qubit gate. It creates superposition from computational basis states: $H|0angle = |+angle$ and $H|1angle = |-angle$. Its matrix is symmetric and unitary: $H =  rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Geometrically, H is a 180° rotation around the axis at 45° between X and Z (the line x=z, y=0). This means $H$ exchanges the X and Z axes: $HXH = Z$ and $HZH = X$. The Hadamard gate is self-inverse: $H^2 = I$, so applying it twice returns to the original state.
keyPoints: Swaps X and Z basis states: HXH = Z, HZH = X
Essential for quantum parallelism and algorithms

sections.title: Phase Gates (S and T)
sections.content: Phase gates rotate the qubit around the Z-axis of the Bloch sphere, changing the relative phase between $|0angle$ and $|1angle$ without changing their magnitudes. The S gate adds a phase of $i$ (90° rotation): $S|0angle = |0angle$, $S|1angle = i|1angle$. The T gate adds a phase of $e^{i\pi/4}$ (45° rotation). These are crucial for creating complex superpositions needed in algorithms. Note that $S = T^2$ and $Z = S^2$, forming a hierarchy: T (π/4), S (π/2), Z (π).

sections.title: Rotation Gates (Rx, Ry, Rz)
sections.content: General rotations around the Bloch sphere axes are parameterized by an angle $	heta$. The rotation gates are: $R_x(	heta) = e^{-i	heta X/2}$, $R_y(	heta) = e^{-i	heta Y/2}$, $R_z(	heta) = e^{-i	heta Z/2}$. Any single-qubit gate can be decomposed into rotations: $U = R_z(\alpha)R_y( eta)R_z(\gamma)$ up to a global phase. This is the Z-Y decomposition. The Pauli gates are special cases: $X = -iR_x(\pi)$, $Y = -iR_y(\pi)$, $Z = -iR_z(\pi)$.
sections.universal: Any single-qubit unitary can be written with 3 parameters: U = e^(iα) Rz(β) Ry(γ) Rz(δ)

sections.title: Universal Gate Sets
sections.content: A set of gates is universal if any quantum computation can be approximated arbitrarily well using only those gates. For single-qubit gates alone, {H, T} is universal—any single-qubit rotation can be approximated. Combined with CNOT (a two-qubit gate), {H, T, CNOT} is universal for all quantum computations. The Solovay-Kitaev theorem states that any single-qubit gate can be approximated to precision $\epsilon$ using $O(\log^c(1/\epsilon))$ gates from a universal set. In practice, quantum computers provide a native gate set and compilers decompose algorithms into these.

keyConcepts.name: Unitarity
keyConcepts.description: Quantum gates must be unitary: $U^\dagger U = I$. This preserves the normalization of quantum states (probabilities sum to 1) and is reversible.
keyConcepts.consequence: All quantum operations are reversible except measurement

keyConcepts.name: Clifford Gates
keyConcepts.description: A group of gates including {H, S, CNOT, Pauli} that map Pauli operators to Pauli operators under conjugation. Classically simulable but essential for error correction.

keyConcepts.name: Euler Decomposition
keyConcepts.description: Any single-qubit gate can be written as $U = e^{i\alpha} R_z( eta) R_y(\gamma) R_z(\delta)$. This shows we need at most 3 rotation parameters plus a global phase.

complexity.timeComplexity: Single-qubit gate: $O(1)$ time on quantum computer
complexity.compilation: Arbitrary rotation approximated to precision ε using $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ Clifford+T gates

steps.title: Initialize Qubit
steps.description: Start with a qubit in state $|0angle$.

steps.title: Apply X Gate (Optional)
steps.description: If needed, flip the bit to start from $|1angle$.

steps.title: Create Superposition with H
steps.description: Apply Hadamard to create an equal superposition.
steps.latex: H|0angle =  rac{|0angle + |1angle}{\sqrt{2}} = |+angle

steps.title: Add Phase with S Gate
steps.description: Rotate around Z-axis to add relative phase.
steps.latex: S|+angle =  rac{|0angle + i|1angle}{\sqrt{2}} = |i+angle

steps.title: Final Rotation with T Gate
steps.description: Apply finer phase rotation for precise state preparation.
steps.latex: T|i+angle =  rac{|0angle + e^{i3\pi/4}|1angle}{\sqrt{2}}

practiceProblems.title: Pauli Gate Composition
practiceProblems.description: What is $XZX$? (Apply X, then Z, then X)
practiceProblems.explanation: XZX = -Z. Since X flips $|0angle \leftrightarrow |1angle$, conjugating Z by X swaps which basis state gets the phase flip. Actually $XZX = |1angle\langle 1| - |0angle\langle 0| = -Z$. Note: global phase -1 is usually ignored.
practiceProblems.hint: Check how XZX acts on |0⟩ and |1⟩.

practiceProblems.title: Hadamard Conjugation
practiceProblems.explanation: $HZH = X$. The Hadamard gate swaps X and Z axes on the Bloch sphere. Conjugating Z by H gives the operator that acts like X (bit flip). Similarly, $HXH = Z$.
practiceProblems.hint: H creates |+⟩ from |0⟩. What operation flips |+⟩ to |−⟩?

practiceProblems.title: Phase Gate Power
practiceProblems.description: How many T gates equal one S gate?
practiceProblems.explanation: $T^2 = S$. T adds phase $e^{i\pi/4}$, S adds phase $e^{i\pi/2} = i$. Since $(e^{i\pi/4})^2 = e^{i\pi/2}$, two T gates equal one S gate.

practiceProblems.title: Rotation Decomposition
practiceProblems.description: Express the X gate using rotation gates: $X = e^{i\alpha} R_z( eta) R_y(\gamma) R_z(\delta)$. What is $\gamma$?
practiceProblems.explanation: X is a 180° rotation around the X-axis. In the Euler decomposition, this requires $\gamma = \pi$ (a rotation around Y by π). Specifically: $X = -i R_z(-\pi/2) R_y(\pi) R_z(\pi/2)$.
practiceProblems.hint: X rotates around the X-axis by 180°. The middle rotation in the decomposition is around Y.

codeExample.python:
import numpy as np

# Define Pauli matrices
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
Y = np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]])
Z = np.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]])
I = np.eye(2)

# Hadamard
H = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]]) / np.sqrt(2)

# Phase gates
S = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1j]])
T = np.array([[1, 0], [0, np.exp(1j * np.pi / 4)]])

# Verify properties
print('Pauli squares equal I:')
print(f'X² = {np.allclose(X @ X, I)}')
print(f'Y² = {np.allclose(Y @ Y, I)}')
print(f'Z² = {np.allclose(Z @ Z, I)}')

print('\nHadamard properties:')
print(f'H² = I: {np.allclose(H @ H, I)}')
print(f'HZH = X: {np.allclose(H @ Z @ H, X)}')
print(f'HXH = Z: {np.allclose(H @ X @ H, Z)}')

print('\nPhase gate relationships:')
print(f'T² = S: {np.allclose(T @ T, S)}')
print(f'S² = Z: {np.allclose(S @ S, Z)}')

# Create rotation matrix
def Rx(theta):
    return np.array([[np.cos(theta/2), -1j*np.sin(theta/2)],
                     [-1j*np.sin(theta/2), np.cos(theta/2)]])

print('\nRotation gate: Rx(π) ≈ X (up to phase)')
print(Rx(np.pi))

import Quipper

gateDemo :: Circ (Bit, Bit)
gateDemo = do
  -- Create two qubits
  q1 <- qinit True   -- |0⟩
  q2 <- qinit True   -- |0⟩
  
  -- Apply gates to q1: X then H
  q1 <- gate_X q1
  q1 <- hadamard q1  -- Now in |-⟩ state
  
  -- Apply gates to q2: H then S then T
  q2 <- hadamard q2
  q2 <- gate_S q2
  q2 <- gate_T q2
  
  -- Measure both
  (q1, b1) <- measure_qubit q1
  (q2, b2) <- measure_qubit q2
  
  return (b1, b2)
